newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss give wary welcome to U.S. Nazi gold report.
newsitem.headline: Swiss give wary welcome to U.S. Nazi gold report.

text.p: Switzerland gave a wary welcome to a U.S. report on Wednesday criticising wartime Swiss gold deals with Nazi Germany, though saying the study lacked historical context, but insisted it would not reopen talks on handing any gold back.

Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti told reporters the mammoth U.S. report would help clear up Switzerland's World War Two history, but added that it appeared to overlook the difficult circumstances Switzerland faced as a small neutral country surrounded by Axis powers.
The report released on Wednesday criticized both the Swiss and American governments of the time for their handling of Nazi gold after the Second World War.
"The Federal Council (cabinet) welcomes the efforts of those responsible for the report to present facts objectively," Cotti said in a statement after the report was released in Washington.
"But on first reading it finds lacking an appropriate appreciation of the extremely difficult situation in which our country found itself at that time, militarily and in terms of supplies."
Cotti said the report also suggested that Germany sold Switzerland gold robbed from invididual Holocaust victims, not just from official stocks, as was believed.

"If this is really true, this a deeply shocking turn of events. It is nearly incomprehensible for us to see the cynicism and cold-bloodedness with which Nazi thugs re-smelted their victims' gold and re-sold it as regular central bank gold," he said.

Cotti and Swiss National Bank (SNB) board member Jean-Pierre Roth said the report also seemed to hold no new revelations that could convince Switzerland to re-open a 1946 accord with the Allies over gold purchases from Germany.

"We have only looked at the report for a very few minutes, but...from the first indications we had today, the Federal Council confirms its attitude that at this moment there is no element for reopening negotiations," Cotti said.

"There is no new fact to say that renegotiation is necessary," Roth added in response to U.S. criticism of Switzerland's hard line in postwar talks with the Allies about returning looted gold it bought.
He reiterated that Switzerland no longer had any Reichsbank gold bars from the period.

Switzerland in 1946 agreed to give the Allies 250 million Swiss francs worth of gold as a voluntary contribution toward the reconstruction of Europe. In return, the Allies agreed to drop any future claims on Switzerland over the gold deals.
Cotti noted that the report gave Switzerland credit for taking steps to probe its wartime history and called on countries to work together to investigate the past.

"We want the truth and justice. Investigations must be conducted openly and without conditions in all countries affected. Switzerland is ready for this and has already introduced the necessary steps," he said.
Washington's ambassador to Switzerland urged both countries to work together to uncover the truth about the era and insisted that "reconciliation rather than confrontation" was the goal.

The report, together with a probe by a panel of historians launched by Berne, will offer a more thorough picture of the Holocaust and the assets Nazis stole from countries and individuals, envoy Madeleine Kunin said.

Thomas Lyssy, vice-president of the Swiss Jewish Federation (SIG), said the most important point in the U.S. report was proof that Nazi gold stocks included victims' gold as well as loot from occupied countries' central banks.
"I am not surprised. I am happy that we now know this and that it is no longer just speculation," Lyssy told Reuters.

Lyssy said the fact that even a small amount of gold stolen from the Nazis came from death camp victims meant that the rest of the German gold claimed by the United States, Britain and France after the war for occupied countries must now go to individuals.
